pantomime

PAN-tuh-mym -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, PAN. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pantomime is acting out meaning through a silent performance of gestures.

Rather than shout across the silent reading room, the twins invented a private pantomime for 'meet me outside.'

Example

The street performer never says a word, yet through pantomime alone the crowd follows an entire story: her hands build an invisible wall, her shoulders sag against an imaginary wind, and when she finally 'opens' a door that is not there, the whole plaza cheers.

Meaning is expressed entirely through gesture, without a single spoken word. Pantomime covers both the everyday act -- miming 'water' across a loud room -- and the theatrical art of telling whole stories in silent movement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

charade: A charade is a pretense -- acting meant to fool people -- or one round of the guessing game charades. A pantomime is honest, wordless communication: the audience is meant to understand every movement, not to be tricked by it.

body language: Body language is the stream of signals your posture, face, and hands give off without your planning any of it. A pantomime is the opposite of accidental: the performer deliberately shapes each movement to build a message or a story.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

speech: communication through spoken words

narration: telling a story aloud in words

Where it sits · how organized the wordless acting is

gesturing → pantomime → mime

gesturing vs. pantomime: Gesturing is the loose, everyday word -- a wave or a shrug is a gesture -- while pantomime organizes gestures into a full message or story that needs no words at all.

mime vs. pantomime: Mime sits at the organized top of this scale: it usually names the trained art or the artist of silent acting, while pantomime covers any wordless acting-out -- from a rehearsed stage show to a game of charades at a birthday party.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — panto-: all, every (Greek pantos)

root — mime: imitator, actor (Greek mimos)

Put it together: Pantomime is Greek for 'imitator of everything' -- pantos ('all') plus mimos ('imitator'). In Roman theaters, a pantomime was a single performer who acted out every role in a story without speaking; the word now names that whole art of meaning made from gesture alone.

Use the root in a new word: mimic: The documentary spent ten full minutes on mimicry among butterflies.

Root Check

Word Choice

Pantomime works two ways: as the silent communication itself ('she used pantomime to order lunch abroad') and as a theatrical performance told through gesture. Either way, the defining rule is no words -- if someone is talking while waving their arms, it is just gesturing, not pantomime.
